01.note: When King Yannai was killing the Sages, Shimon ben Shatah was hidden by his sister, the king's wife, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perahya fled to Alexandria in Egypt. Once peace was made, Shimon ben Shatah wrote to him as if Jerusalem were writing to Alexandria: my husband dwells with you and I sit desolate. On the way home, at an inn, the rabbi praised the place, and his student Jesus the Nazarene remarked that the innkeeper's wife had narrow eyes. Calling him wicked, the rabbi excommunicated him and turned him away day after day; when he finally signaled during Shema that he would take him back, Jesus thought he was rejected, set up a brick and worshipped it, and would not repent, citing his teacher's own rule.
01.why: Elisha's failed attempt to bring back Gehazi has just been told, and Gehazi answered with the same rule about one who makes the masses sin. Both are teachers who pushed a student away, and the Gemara follows with the teaching that the left hand should push away while the right draws near.

people.name: Yehoshua ben Perahya
people.about: A Sage who fled to Alexandria and later excommunicated his student Jesus.

people.name: Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: A Sage hidden by his sister, King Yannai's wife, who wrote to recall Yehoshua ben Perahya.

people.name: King Yannai
people.about: The king who was killing the Sages.

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: A student of Yehoshua ben Perahya, excommunicated by him.

terms.meaning: Rams' horns. Here four hundred were brought out as part of a formal, public excommunication.
Placed under a ban that cut the person off from the community and from his teacher.
The declaration of God's oneness, recited morning and evening, which one does not interrupt to speak.

02.note: Yohanan the High Priest had sent messengers across the land and learned that people set aside the main priestly portion of their crops but were careless with the tithes. He gathered them and said: My sons, eating untithed produce, or the priest's share of the tithe, carries a death penalty from Heaven, just as the main priestly portion does. He then made an ordinance: whoever buys produce from an unlearned person must set aside first and second tithe himself, give the priest's share of the first tithe to a priest, and eat the second tithe in Jerusalem. But a Levite or a poor person claiming the first tithe or the poor man's tithe must bring proof.
02.why: The Gemara has asked whether people still tithed in Yohanan the High Priest's day, since he canceled the declaration of tithes. This baraita shows many did not, and the Gemara resolves it: he made two ordinances, one for the careful and one for produce bought from the unlearned.

terms.meaning: The main priestly portion, the first share of a crop given to a priest.
The tenth of the Levite's first tithe that the Levite must pass on to a priest.
An unlearned person, not trusted to have set aside the required tithes.
A tenth of the crop that the owner brings to Jerusalem and eats there.

02.flag: The story opens mid-baraita: the speaker is unnamed and his investigation, which prompts his words, sits in the preceding BEFORE segment.

03.note: Rav Huna taught that the songs of men hauling ships or leading herds are permitted, but the singing of weavers is forbidden. Later Rav Huna banned all song, and food became so plentiful that a hundred ducks, or a hundred se'a of wheat, sold for a dinar and no one wanted them. Then Rav Hisda came and made light of the ban, and afterward a single duck could not be found even for a dinar.
03.why: The mishna says song was banned after the Sanhedrin ceased, and Rav and Rava have just warned that song in a house brings its ruin. Rav Huna's ban, and what happened when it lapsed, illustrates that warning in prices.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who first permitted work songs and later banned all song.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who came after and made light of Rav Huna's ban.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume for grain, roughly several liters.
A silver coin; a hundred ducks for one dinar means food was almost free.

04.note: Once the Sages were reclining in an upper room of the house of Gurya in Jericho when a Divine Voice announced that one of them was worthy of the Divine Presence resting on him, but his generation was not fit for it. They looked at Hillel the Elder, and when he died they eulogized him: Alas pious one, alas humble one, student of Ezra. The same thing happened in Yavne, and they looked at Shmuel HaKatan, mourned as a student of Hillel. As he was dying, Shmuel HaKatan foretold that Shimon and Yishmael would go to the sword, their colleagues to killing and the people to plunder. The Sages wanted to eulogize Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava the same way, but the times were too troubled, since those killed by the monarchy were not eulogized.
04.why: A baraita has just said that after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi died the Divine Spirit left Israel, but the Sages still received guidance through a Divine Voice. These scenes are its proof.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: The Sage the others looked to in Jericho, eulogized as a student of Ezra.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: The Sage singled out in Yavne, eulogized as a student of Hillel; he foretold coming killings.

people.name: Shimon
people.about: Named by Shmuel HaKatan as destined for the sword; the translation identifies him as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

people.name: Yishmael
people.about: Named with Shimon as destined for the sword; the translation identifies him as Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: A Sage killed by the monarchy, whom the Sages could not eulogize.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that the Sages heard after prophecy had ended.
God's presence resting on a person, the mark of a prophet.

05.note: Rav Huna found a fragrant date and wrapped it in his shawl. His son Rabba came in and said he could smell a fragrant date. Rav Huna told him, My son, there is purity in you, and gave it to him. Then Rabba's own son Abba arrived, and Rabba gave the date to him. Rav Huna said to Rabba: My son, you have made my heart rejoice and you have blunted my teeth. The Gemara adds the folk saying that a father's love goes to his sons, and the sons' love to their own sons.
05.why: The mishna said that since the Temple was destroyed fruit has lost its taste, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar has just taught that lost purity took away taste and aroma. Rabba's ability to smell the date is read as a sign of that purity.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The father who found the date and gave it to his son.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Rav Huna's son, who smelled the date and gave it to his own son.

people.name: Abba
people.about: Rabba's son, who received the date.

terms.meaning: An expression of hurt: Rav Huna was pained that his son passed the gift to the grandson rather than back to him.

06.note: Rav Aha bar Yaakov raised Rav Yaakov, his daughter's son. When the boy had grown up, his grandfather asked him for a drink of water, and the grandson answered: I am not your son. The Gemara attaches the folk saying: raise him, raise him, and he will say, I am your daughter's son.
06.why: It follows directly on the story of Rav Huna, his son and grandson, which ended with a saying that a son's love goes to his own sons. This second incident adds a saying about how a grandchild repays the grandparent who raised him.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who raised his daughter's son.

people.name: Rav Yaakov
people.about: Rav Aha bar Yaakov's grandson, who refused him water once grown.

07.note: Rabba bar Rav Huna made a tambourine for his son. His father, Rav Huna, came and broke it, saying it could be confused with a one-mouthed drum. He told him to make one instead over the mouth of an earthen jug or of a small kefiza measuring vessel.
07.why: The mishna lists a decree against drums from the war of Vespasian, and Rabbi Elazar has just defined that drum as one with a single mouth. Rav Huna's act shows the ban applied even to a toy that might look like one.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Made a tambourine for his son.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rabba's father, who broke the tambourine.

terms.meaning: A drum with a skin on one side only, the instrument the Sages banned.
A small unit of measure; here, the small vessel used to measure it, over which a toy drum could be made.

08.note: When the Hasmonean kings fought each other, Hyrcanus besieged Jerusalem with Aristobulus inside. Each day those inside lowered coins in a box, and those outside sent up animals for the daily Temple offerings. An elder who knew Greek wisdom told the besiegers, in that Greek wisdom, that as long as the Temple service went on the city would not fall to them. The next day they sent up a pig. Halfway up the wall it dug in its hooves, and the land of Israel shook for four hundred parasangs. At that time the Sages said: cursed is one who raises pigs, and cursed is one who teaches his son Greek wisdom. That year the omer had to come from Gaggot Tzerifim and the two loaves from the valley of Ein Sokher.
08.why: The mishna lists a decree that a man may not teach his son Greek, and this baraita gives its origin. The Gemara then asks how that fits with Sages who praised the Greek language, and answers that the language and Greek wisdom are separate things.

people.name: Hyrcanus
people.about: A Hasmonean king, besieging Jerusalem from outside.

people.name: Aristoblus
people.about: A Hasmonean king, besieged inside Jerusalem.

terms.meaning: The two lambs offered in the Temple every day, morning and afternoon.
A Persian measure of distance, a few miles.
The measure of barley offered in the Temple on the second day of Passover.
The two wheat loaves offered in the Temple on Shavuot.

09.note: A man borrowed an ax from another man and broke it. He came before Rav, who told him: go and pay him with a good, whole ax. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi asked Rav, Is this the law? and Rav was silent.
09.why: The Gemara is unsure whether, by Shmuel's account, a court values a broken item for a borrower, so the owner takes it back and the borrower pays only the loss. Rav's order first seems to say no; his silence before his students is read as yes, and the law follows them.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who ordered the borrower to replace the ax.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling, with Rav Asi.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling, with Rav Kahana.

terms.meaning: When a court appraises a damaged item, the owner keeps the item at its reduced value and the one responsible pays only the difference.

10.note: A donkey ate some bread and broke the basket it was kept in. Rav Yehuda ruled that its owner must pay the full damage for the bread but only half the damage for the basket.
10.why: The Gemara is sorting animal damage into normal eating, which costs full damages, and unusual acts, which cost half. Asked why the basket is not part of eating, it answers that the donkey ate first and only then broke the basket.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the donkey's damage.

terms.meaning: An owner pays the whole loss when his animal does harm in its normal way, such as eating; for an unusual act, like goring, by an animal not known for it, he pays half.

11.note: A goat saw a turnip on top of a clay barrel. It climbed up, ate the turnip, and broke the barrel. Rava made its owner pay full damages for both the turnip and the barrel.
11.why: The Gemara has just explained why a donkey that broke a basket after eating cost only half. Here it explains Rava's full award: since a goat normally eats turnips, climbing to reach one is normal too, so the broken barrel counts as part of eating.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled the goat's owner fully liable.

terms.meaning: Payment of the whole loss, owed when an animal does harm in its normal way, as when eating.

12.note: Rami bar Hama told Rav Hisda that the question he had raised was already answered in a mishna. Rav Hisda asked which mishna, and Rami bar Hama said he would tell him after Rav Hisda served him. Rav Hisda took Rami bar Hama's scarf and folded it, and Rami bar Hama then quoted it: if the animal benefits, its owner pays for the benefit it derived.
12.why: The question is whether a squatter in a courtyard that would never have been rented must pay for the benefit he got, though the owner lost nothing. Rami bar Hama offers the mishna as the answer, and Rava then remarks that the two cases are not really alike.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The Sage who said a mishna answered the question, once he had been served.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage who asked, and folded Rami bar Hama's scarf as a service.

terms.meaning: The earliest written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

13.note: A man built a mansion on a garbage heap that belonged to orphans. Before that, nomadic Carmanians had lived on the site and paid the orphans a small sum. Rav Nahman told the man to go and appease the orphans, but he paid no attention, so Rav Nahman confiscated his mansion.
13.why: The Gemara has cited Rav's view that one who lives in another's courtyard without permission need not pay rent. It asks whether Rav Nahman's ruling disagrees, and answers no: here the orphans lost real income from the Carmanians.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who told the builder to appease the orphans and then confiscated his mansion.

terms.meaning: Nomadic tribespeople who had lived on the orphans' land and paid them a little for it.

14.note: Two people shared a cistern and took turns drawing water from it, one each day. One of them came to draw on a day that was not his. The other said, This is my day, but he paid no attention, so the other took the handle of a hoe and struck him. Rav Hisda sent the case to Rav Nahman, who answered that he should have struck him a hundred times with the hoe.
14.why: Rav Hisda had asked what fine applies to a blow with a hoe, and Rav Nahman wanted the facts first. His answer leads into the dispute over taking justice into one's own hands, which, Rav Nahman says, everyone allows when a loss would otherwise follow.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage who sent the case of the cistern to Rav Nahman.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who said the striker was right to strike.

terms.term: Take justice into one's own hands
terms.meaning: To enforce one's own rights directly, without going to a court first.

15.note: A man slapped another. Rav Toviya bar Mattana asked Rav Yosef whether the sela fine set for a slap means the valuable Tyrian sela or the small provincial one. They argued it from a mishna about a gold dinar, and it was settled by Rav's rule, quoted by Rav Yehuda: coins in the Torah are Tyrian, coins in the Sages' rulings are provincial, so the fine is half a dinar. The man who was slapped said that for so little he did not want it; let it go to the poor. Then he changed his mind and asked for it to live on. Rav Yosef told him the poor had already acquired it, since the court acts as the hand of the poor.
15.why: The Gemara has turned to a mishna that sets a sela as the fine for a slap, against Rabbi Yehuda's hundred dinars; this case fixes what that sela is worth. Rav Yosef's last ruling leads into the rule that a court likewise acts for orphans.

people.name: Rav Toviya bar Mattana
people.about: A Sage who sent the slapping case to Rav Yosef and argued with his answer.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who answered, and ruled the fine belonged to the poor.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Quoted Rav's rule on Torah and rabbinic coinage.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose rule on coinage settled the question.

terms.meaning: A silver coin. A Tyrian sela was worth four dinars; a provincial sela only half a dinar.
A Sage of the mishna's era; here, the author of the mishna.
The court acts as the legal agent of the poor, so it can take possession for them.

16.note: Hanan the wicked slapped a man, and the case came before Rav Huna, who told him to go and pay the man half a dinar. Hanan had a clipped dinar and wanted to pay half of it, but no one would take it to give him change. So he slapped the man again and gave him the whole clipped dinar.
16.why: The Gemara has just fixed the fine for a slap at a provincial sela, half a dinar. This second slapping case shows that sum ordered in practice.

people.name: Hanan the wicked
people.about: A man who slapped another, then slapped him again.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who fined Hanan half a dinar.

terms.meaning: A coin with its edge trimmed, which people were unwilling to accept or change.

17.note: The Roman kingdom once sent two military officials to the Sages of Israel with the order: Teach us your Torah. They read it, and read it again, and a third time. As they left, they said they had examined the whole Torah and found it true, except one rule: a Jew's ox that gores a gentile's ox is exempt, while a gentile's ox that gores a Jew's ox pays full damages, whether innocuous or forewarned. The story as given here ends with their objection.
17.why: The Gemara has been discussing gentiles and the commandments, and the Sages tell this baraita in connection with the rule on a Jew's ox and a gentile's ox. It records the one point that outsiders who accepted the rest of the Torah could not accept.

terms.meaning: An innocuous ox has not gored before, so its owner pays half; a forewarned ox has gored three times, so its owner pays in full.

17.flag: Cut short: the officials' reasoning and their decision not to tell the kingdom, which complete the story, are in the next (AFTER) segment.

18.note: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's daughter died. The Sages asked Ulla to come with them to console him, but Ulla refused: the Babylonian words of comfort, What can be done?, are heresy, as if they would act if they could. He went alone and told Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda about Moses. God told Moses not to fight Moab, because Moses had reasoned that if the Midianites, who only helped Moab, were to be attacked, Moab itself deserved it all the more. God answered that He had other thoughts: He had two good fledglings to bring out of them, Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. The story as given ends here, before Ulla draws the comfort from it.
18.why: It is introduced as an aside right after the account of the Roman officials. Its verse about Moab leads into the teaching that God withholds no creature's reward, which the Gemara also draws from Moab.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose daughter died.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage who refused the Babylonian way of consoling and went alone to comfort him.

people.name: Moses
people.about: Reasoned that Moab should be fought, and was told not to.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who explained to Moses why Moab was spared.

terms.meaning: Reasoning from a lighter case to a weightier one: if this holds for the lesser, all the more for the greater.
Young birds; here a figure for two women, Ruth and Naamah, who would come from Moab and Ammon.

18.flag: Cut short: Ulla's application of the lesson to the dead daughter, which completes the consolation, is in the next (AFTER) segment.

19.note: Shimon HaAmasoni, or by another account Nehemya HaAmasoni, drew a lesson from every occurrence of the word et in the Torah. When he reached You shall fear et the Lord your God, he stopped. His students asked what would become of all the interpretations he had already made. He said: just as I received reward for expounding, I receive reward for withdrawing. Later Rabbi Akiva came and taught that et in that verse includes Torah scholars.
19.why: The Gemara has explained that one tanna derives the ban on a stoned ox's hide from the word et, while another does not read et for new rules at all. This baraita shows that method of reading and the point where it was abandoned.

people.name: Shimon HaAmasoni
people.about: A Sage who interpreted every et in the Torah until he reached the fear of God.

people.name: Nehemya HaAmasoni
people.about: The name some give the same Sage.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Later taught that the et in the verse includes Torah scholars.

terms.meaning: A small Hebrew word that marks the object of a verb and is not translated. Some Sages read each occurrence as adding something to the verse.

20.note: A woman went into a house to bake. The homeowner's goat came and ate her dough, became overheated and died. Rava made the woman pay for the goat.
20.why: The Gemara is asking who is liable when one person's animal or goods are on another's property. It asks whether Rava's ruling clashes with Rav, who exempts produce brought in without permission, and answers that she came in with permission and so took on responsibility.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who made the woman pay for the goat.
